statement: A fair coin is tossed four times. What is the probability of getting at least two heads?

choices.misconception: I worked out the probability of exactly two heads and forgot about three and four heads.
I thought heads and tails are equally likely, so at least two heads must happen half of the time.
I listed the five possible numbers of heads, 0 to 4, and treated them as equally likely, so three out of five count.
I found the probability of at least one head instead of at least two heads.

hints: There are 16 equally likely sequences. Which ones fail?
Count the sequences directly by their number of heads, then check by counting the complement: the sequences with fewer than two heads. Two methods agreeing is your safety net.
Sequences with no heads: 1. Sequences with exactly one head: 4.

solutions.reliable: Of the 16 equally likely sequences, 6 have exactly two heads, 4 have three and 1 has four, so 11 have at least two heads and the probability is 11/16. Check with the complement: 1 sequence has no heads and 4 have exactly one, so 16 - 5 = 11 again. The transferable idea: a second method, here the complement, catches the slips that the first method invites.
solutions.elegant: The complement is the quicker route: 1 - (1 + 4)/16 = 11/16.

whyOnTest: Probability questions punish one-method answers; a complement check catches the exactly-two, at-least-one and equally-likely-counts traps.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
